docs.title: 6.5 XR, Cloud Gaming and the Uplink Challenge
docs.text:
Extended reality (XR) — virtual, augmented and mixed reality — and cloud gaming need steady high data rates with low, predictable latency in both directions. Most networks are built for downloading, so uploads (camera feeds, game inputs, pose data, live streams) are often the bottleneck. 5G-Advanced Release 18 added features specifically for XR traffic.

What different apps ask of the network

Downlink Uplink Latency need Video streaming High Very low Relaxed (buffering) Cloud gaming High (15-50 Mbit/s) Low but constant Tight (<50 ms RTT) Split-rendered VR Very high Moderate (pose, sensors) Very tight (~20 ms) AR glasses Moderate High (camera to edge AI) Tight Live creator stream Low High (5-20 Mbit/s) Moderate

XR and creators stress the uplink and latency, not just download speed.

Think of it like…

Most mobile networks are like a one-way street with a narrow cycle lane going the other way: perfect for deliveries in, awkward when everyone wants to send things out.

Real-world example

Kofi plays a cloud racing game on a tablet over 5G. Each controller input travels up to an edge server, the frame renders, and video streams back. With a 25 ms round trip it feels local; when his neighbour starts live-streaming, uplink congestion pushes latency to 120 ms and Kofi's car drifts into walls.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. XR devices send pose and sensor data upwards continuously and receive rendered video or scene updates downwards.
  2. Split rendering moves heavy graphics to an edge server, keeping the headset light but requiring tight latency.
  3. Traffic is bursty: each video frame arrives as a burst of packets every 8-17 ms (60-120 frames per second).
  4. Rel-18 features let the network understand 'PDU sets' (packets of one frame), discard late packets and align sleep cycles to frame timing.
  5. Uplink is improved with more uplink slots, supplementary uplink, uplink MIMO, carrier aggregation and, in future, sub-band full duplex.

Who uses it

XR and game-streaming engineers, RAN performance specialists, edge-computing teams and device makers.

Key takeaway

Remember the comfort rule of thumb for VR: motion-to-photon latency should stay below about 20 ms, or users risk motion sickness.

Going deeper

  • Typical 5G TDD patterns such as DDDSU or DDDDDDDSUU give roughly 20-30% of time to uplink, and phones transmit at much lower power than base stations, so uplink capacity and coverage are fundamentally scarcer.
  • Rel-18 XR enhancements introduced PDU-set-aware QoS (treating all packets of a video frame as a unit), PDU-set discard when a frame is too late, XR-friendly DRX cycles matching non-integer frame periods, and configured-grant improvements.
  • Rel-18 also enabled L4S (Low Latency, Low Loss, Scalable throughput, IETF RFC 9330-9332) support, letting the RAN mark congestion so applications reduce bitrate before queues and latency build up.
  • Uplink boosters include supplementary uplink (SUL) on low bands, uplink carrier aggregation, Tx switching between carriers, two-layer uplink MIMO in phones, and Rel-18/19 sub-band full duplex (SBFD) studies and work.
  • Cloud-gaming services such as Xbox Cloud Gaming and Nvidia GeForce NOW run on data centres; mobile users benefit most when servers are regionally close and the radio link is lightly loaded.
  • Headsets such as Meta Quest 3 and Apple Vision Pro mostly use Wi-Fi today; smart glasses with cameras and AI assistants are the more likely early driver of cellular XR uplink demand.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Judging XR readiness by download speed tests: latency jitter and uplink capacity matter more for interactive experiences.
  • Assuming edge computing alone fixes latency: radio scheduling and queueing often dominate the delay budget.
  • Forgetting battery and heat: continuous uplink transmission drains phones and glasses quickly.

docs.title: 6.6 Public Safety and Mission-Critical Services: MCPTT, FirstNet, ESN
docs.text:
Police, fire and ambulance services need radios that work in disasters, give them priority over the public, and support instant group voice ('push-to-talk'). 3GPP's mission-critical services (MCPTT for voice, MCData and MCVideo) bring this to LTE and 5G, replacing older systems such as TETRA and P25. The US FirstNet and South Korea's Safe-Net are running; the UK's ESN has been repeatedly delayed.

A mission-critical push-to-talk group call. Floor control ensures only one person talks at a time, with priority override.

Think of it like…

It is like a city's ambulance lanes: normally shared roads, but with sirens on, emergency vehicles get priority and can push other traffic aside.

Real-world example

During a wildfire in a fictional Californian county, 300 firefighters use FirstNet phones. A battalion chief presses push-to-talk and all crews in the 'Division A' group hear her within a fraction of a second. Despite thousands of residents calling relatives, responders' traffic gets priority and pre-emption, and a deployable cell on a truck covers a burnt-out valley.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Responders' devices register with priority subscriptions and join pre-defined talk groups.
  2. A user presses push-to-talk; the device asks the MCPTT server for the 'floor' (permission to speak).
  3. The server grants the floor and media flows to all group members, often over multicast in busy cells.
  4. The network applies priority and pre-emption (QoS class and allocation-retention priority) to keep calls up under load.
  5. Where networks fail, deployable cells, satellite backhaul or direct device-to-device modes keep teams connected.

Who uses it

Public-safety communications officers, critical-communications engineers, operators' government units and vendors such as Motorola Solutions and Airbus.

Key takeaway

Know the trio: MCPTT (Rel-13, 2016) for voice, MCData and MCVideo (Rel-14) — together called MCX or mission-critical services.

Going deeper

  • MCPTT targets mouth-to-ear latency under about 300 ms and access time under 300 ms; it supports group, private, emergency and imminent-peril calls with priority override.
  • FirstNet, the US public-safety broadband network, is built and run by AT&T under a 25-year contract (2017) with the FirstNet Authority, using Band 14 (700 MHz) plus AT&T bands; it passed 7 million connections in early 2025.
  • The UK Emergency Services Network (ESN), planned to replace the TETRA-based Airwave network, has suffered long delays; Airwave's December 2026 shutdown target was widely expected to slip, with ESN completion discussed for around 2029-2030.
  • South Korea's Safe-Net, a PS-LTE network in 700 MHz, launched nationally in 2021; other countries such as Finland (Virve 2.0) and France (RRF) are moving public safety onto shared commercial networks with priority.
  • Resilience tools include Isolated E-UTRAN Operation for Public Safety (IOPS) for base stations cut off from the core, ProSe off-network direct mode, deployable systems and satellite backhaul.
  • Commercial 5G slices now target responders too: T-Mobile's T-Priority (5G SA slice, launched 2024-2025) and Verizon Frontline offerings compete with FirstNet in the US.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming LTE replaced TETRA/P25 overnight: most agencies run both for years, using interworking gateways during migration.
  • Equating priority with guaranteed coverage: priority does not help where there is no signal, so deployables and direct mode matter.
  • Underestimating device ecosystems: rugged MCX-certified handsets and accessories take years to mature.

docs.title: 6.7 Positioning: From E911 to Centimetre-Level 5G Location
docs.text:
Mobile networks can work out where a device is, not just connect it. Early methods only knew which cell you were in; 5G measures signal timing and angles from several base stations, and 5G-Advanced adds carrier-phase techniques for centimetre accuracy. Uses include emergency calls, factories, logistics and indoor navigation where satellite positioning fails.

Positioning accuracy targets (approximate). Each generation of 3GPP features tightened accuracy by about an order of magnitude.

Think of it like…

It is like locating a thunderstorm by counting seconds between flash and thunder from several friends' houses — combine the timings and you can pinpoint it.

Real-world example

In a fictional logistics hub in Rotterdam, GPS fails under the steel roof. A private 5G network measures uplink signal arrival times at 12 indoor radios and locates each forklift within 50 cm, so the warehouse system knows which pallet each one picked up.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The location server (LMF in 5G) receives a request, for example from an emergency call or an industrial app.
  2. It asks base stations to send positioning reference signals (PRS) or measure the device's sounding reference signals (SRS).
  3. The device or network measures time differences, round-trip times or angles of arrival/departure.
  4. The LMF combines measurements with known antenna positions to calculate location (or the device does, with assistance data).
  5. The position is delivered to the requester with an accuracy estimate.

Who uses it

Location-services engineers, emergency-call regulators, industrial IoT designers and indoor-navigation developers.

Key takeaway

Remember the 5G positioning methods: DL-TDOA, UL-TDOA, multi-RTT, DL-AoD, UL-AoA and NR E-CID — plus GNSS assistance.

Going deeper

  • Rel-16 NR positioning targeted horizontal accuracy below 3 m indoors and 10 m outdoors for 80% of devices; Rel-17 tightened commercial targets to sub-metre and industrial IoT to 0.2 m with lower latency.
  • The LTE Positioning Protocol (LPP, TS 37.355) runs between device and location server, while NRPPa carries measurements between gNB and LMF; the LMF is a 5G core network function introduced in Rel-15/16.
  • Multi-RTT measures round-trip times to several base stations, avoiding the need for tight network synchronisation, while TDOA methods require well-synchronised cells.
  • Rel-18 added carrier-phase positioning (measuring the phase of the carrier for centimetre-level ranging), sidelink positioning, low-power high-accuracy positioning and positioning for RedCap devices.
  • In the US, FCC E911 rules require location for wireless 911 calls, including vertical (z-axis) location within 3 m for 80% of indoor calls in top markets; dispatchable addresses are increasingly delivered from devices.
  • Cellular networks also deliver GNSS assistance (A-GNSS) and RTK correction data via LPP, speeding up satellite fixes and enabling centimetre-level GNSS for drones and machinery.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming 5G phones are located to centimetres today: high-accuracy methods need dense, synchronised deployments and supporting devices.
  • Ignoring multipath indoors: reflections in factories distort timing measurements without line-of-sight detection and AI-assisted methods.
  • Forgetting privacy: continuous location tracking requires consent, lawful basis and careful data handling.

docs.title: Try it: Toy multi-RTT positioning: find a point from three measured distances
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import least_squares
gnbs = np.array([[0, 0], [100, 0], [0, 80]])        # antenna positions (m)
rtt_ns = np.array([520.7, 426.9, 447.2])             # measured round-trip times (true point: 60, 50)
dist = rtt_ns * 1e-9 * 3e8 / 2                       # metres
res = least_squares(lambda p: np.linalg.norm(gnbs - p, axis=1) - dist, x0=[50, 40])
print("Estimated position (m):", res.x.round(1))

docs.title: 6.8 Broadcast and Multicast: 5G Broadcast, NR MBS and Public Warnings
docs.text:
Normal mobile data is 'unicast': one copy of a video per viewer. Broadcast sends one stream that any number of devices can receive, like TV. 5G Broadcast lets TV and radio companies transmit to phones from tall towers, even to phones without a SIM, while NR multicast/broadcast services (MBS) let operators send one stream to many users inside the mobile network. Emergency alerts use a related, older mechanism called cell broadcast.

Three ways to deliver one stream to many

5G Broadcast NR MBS DVB-T2 Based on LTE FeMBMS (Rel-14/16+) 5G NR (Rel-17+) DVB (ETSI) Who runs it Broadcasters, tower firms Mobile operators Broadcasters SIM needed No (receive-only mode) Yes No Coverage Large HPHT towers Mobile cells Large HPHT towers Receivers Few phones in 2026 5G SA phones with support TVs, set-top boxes

5G Broadcast competes with DVB-T2 for TV distribution; NR MBS serves operators' own services.

Think of it like…

Unicast is phoning each friend to tell them the news; broadcast is announcing it over a stadium loudspeaker — the cost is the same whether ten or ten thousand people listen.

Real-world example

A fictional public broadcaster in Bavaria trials 5G Broadcast from its existing TV towers at 600 MHz. Commuters with compatible phones watch a live football match on the train without using their data allowance, and the network load stays the same whether 500 or 50,000 people tune in.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Content is encoded once and sent to broadcast transmitters or base stations.
  2. 5G Broadcast uses high-power, high-tower (HPHT) transmitters covering large areas, in receive-only mode with no uplink or SIM needed.
  3. NR MBS (Rel-17) runs inside the operator's 5G network, delivering one stream to a group of users in a cell or area.
  4. Devices with supporting chipsets and apps tune in to the broadcast or multicast session.
  5. Public warnings use cell broadcast to push alerts to every phone in selected cells within seconds.

Who uses it

Broadcast network operators, public broadcasters, operators' video teams, emergency-alert authorities and chipset vendors.

Key takeaway

Do not confuse the two: '5G Broadcast' is the LTE-based terrestrial broadcast system (evolved from FeMBMS) for broadcasters; 'NR MBS' is multicast/broadcast inside 5G NR networks.

Going deeper

  • 5G Broadcast evolved from LTE eMBMS via 'FeMBMS' in Rel-14 and enhancements in Rel-16 that met IMT-2020 requirements; it supports a receive-only mode, free-to-air reception and long cyclic prefixes for large single-frequency networks.
  • Later releases added broadcaster-friendly channel bandwidths of 6, 7 and 8 MHz in the UHF TV band, and Rel-19 work added robustness features such as time-frequency interleaving for mobile reception.
  • European broadcasters and tower companies (for example Media Broadcast, TDF and Rohde & Schwarz in the 5G Broadcast Strategic Task Force) have targeted commercial services around 2027; Vantage Towers signed with Rohde & Schwarz to support rollout from 2026.
  • The biggest hurdle is receivers: smartphones need 5G Broadcast support in their chipsets and software, and few models had it enabled by 2026.
  • NR MBS (Rel-17) supports point-to-multipoint delivery in connected mode, with Rel-18 adding reception in RRC_INACTIVE and other enhancements, useful for live venues, software updates and group communications.
  • Cell broadcast (3GPP TS 23.041) underpins public warning systems such as the US Wireless Emergency Alerts, EU-Alert and the UK Emergency Alerts system launched in 2023.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming every 5G phone can receive 5G Broadcast: it needs specific chipset support and software that most phones lacked in 2026.
  • Confusing cell broadcast alerts with SMS: alerts are broadcast to all phones in an area without knowing numbers and do not congest the network.
  • Expecting broadcast to replace streaming apps: it suits big live events and linear channels, not personalised on-demand viewing.

docs.title: 6.9 Healthcare, Agriculture, Smart Cities and Drones: Hype vs Reality
docs.text:
5G marketing promised remote surgery, robot farms and smart cities. By 2026, the reality is more modest: valuable but specific uses such as connected ambulances, remote patient monitoring, precision agriculture with sensors and drones, and city cameras. Many 'smart' projects use 4G, LTE-M, NB-IoT, fibre or Wi-Fi rather than 5G, and coverage and business cases matter more than peak speed.

Vertical use cases and their 2026 reality. Most successes need coverage and integration more than gigabit speeds.

Think of it like…

5G in verticals is like a powerful new kitchen appliance: impressive in the showroom, but at home people use it for a few things they really need, not every recipe in the brochure.

Real-world example

Dr Okoro runs a fictional rural health network in Ghana. Ambulances send ECGs and video to the regional hospital over 4G and 5G, and diabetic patients use connected glucose monitors. A 5G remote-surgery demo impressed visitors, but the hospital's real gains came from faster triage and fewer unnecessary transfers.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Identify a problem worth solving (response times, crop yields, energy waste), not a technology to deploy.
  2. Check coverage where the use happens — fields, roads, inside hospitals — and pick the right connectivity (NB-IoT, LTE-M, 5G, private network, satellite).
  3. Integrate with existing systems: hospital records, farm management software, city platforms.
  4. Address regulation, privacy, safety certification and staff training.
  5. Measure outcomes and costs; scale only what pays off.

Who uses it

Digital-health teams, agritech companies, city IT departments, drone operators and operators' enterprise sales teams.

Key takeaway

In interviews, show balance: name one real 5G vertical success (e.g. connected ambulances or FWA for farms) and one over-hyped example (e.g. routine remote surgery over public networks).

Going deeper

  • Remote surgery demonstrations over 5G attracted headlines from about 2019, but routine telesurgery remains rare because of liability, regulation and the need for guaranteed, redundant connectivity.
  • Connected ambulances stream vital signs and video to emergency departments so specialists can prepare or redirect patients; these often use multi-operator bonded 4G/5G routers rather than a single network.
  • Agriculture suffers from rural coverage gaps: many farms use LoRaWAN, NB-IoT where available, or satellite (for example tractors connected via LEO satellite services) alongside 4G/5G FWA for the farmhouse.
  • Smart-city projects often fail on business models: sensors are cheap, but integration, maintenance and data platforms are not; successful projects focus on narrow goals like parking enforcement or street-light energy savings.
  • 3GPP added UAV (drone) support in Rel-15 to Rel-18, including drone identification, flight-path reporting and interference handling, because airborne phones see many cells and cause uplink interference.
  • Utilities increasingly deploy private LTE/5G for grid automation, often in dedicated spectrum such as 410-430 MHz in Europe or 900 MHz in the US.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming a vertical needs 5G because it is 'digital': many IoT use cases are cheaper and better on NB-IoT, LTE-M, LoRaWAN or fibre.
  • Building pilots without an owner for scaling: many 5G city and hospital trials ended when grant funding stopped.
  • Ignoring regulation: medical devices, drones and critical infrastructure need certification beyond connectivity.

docs.title: 6.10 Network APIs and Monetisation: CAMARA, GSMA Open Gateway and Aduna
docs.text:
Network APIs let app developers ask the mobile network simple questions or request services through a web API — 'Is this phone number really on this device?', 'Was the SIM swapped recently?', 'Give this video call better quality for ten minutes'. CAMARA writes the open API definitions, GSMA Open Gateway gets operators to offer them consistently, and aggregators such as Aduna sell access across many operators.

Silent login with the Number Verification API. The operator confirms the number from the device's own mobile data session — no SMS code.

Think of it like…

Network APIs are like a hotel concierge desk: instead of guests wandering into the kitchen or the security office, they ask the concierge, who answers using information only the hotel has.

Real-world example

Fictional bank NovaBank checks the SIM Swap API before approving a large transfer. If the customer's SIM changed in the last 24 hours — a common sign of fraud — the app asks for extra verification. Login uses the Number Verification API, so customers no longer wait for SMS codes that criminals could intercept.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. CAMARA (a Linux Foundation project) defines API specifications in OpenAPI format, released in twice-yearly 'meta-releases'.
  2. Operators implement the APIs on their networks, exposing data from the core (e.g. via NEF) behind secure gateways.
  3. Developers access APIs through an operator directly, a hyperscaler marketplace or an aggregator such as Aduna or Vonage.
  4. Authorisation uses OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect, with user consent where personal data is involved.
  5. The app calls the API, gets an answer, and the operator charges per call or by subscription.

Who uses it

API product managers, fraud-prevention and identity teams, developers, operator wholesale units and aggregators.

Key takeaway

Know the three layers: CAMARA = API specifications, GSMA Open Gateway = operator commitment and branding, aggregators (Aduna, Vonage, Infobip and others) = one contract for many operators.

Going deeper

  • CAMARA was launched in 2022 by the GSMA and the Linux Foundation; its Fall25 meta-release contained 60 APIs (10 stable, 27 updated, 23 new), covering identity, fraud, location, quality and device status.
  • GSMA Open Gateway launched at MWC 2023 with eight APIs; by May 2025, 73 operator groups (almost 80% of connections) had joined, and in 2026 GSMA reported 300+ commercial launches of 20 CAMARA APIs in 65 markets.
  • Aduna, a joint venture of Ericsson (50%) and a dozen large operators including AT&T, Deutsche Telekom, Orange, Telefónica, T-Mobile, Verizon and Vodafone, began operating in 2025 under CEO Anthony Bartolo to aggregate network APIs globally.
  • Fraud and identity APIs (Number Verification, SIM Swap, KYC Match) have the strongest early demand from banks and payment firms; Quality on Demand has proven harder to sell because it needs 5G SA and end-to-end QoS support.
  • Inside the network, APIs are typically implemented using the 5G core's Network Exposure Function (NEF) and SCEF in 4G, plus operator systems such as HLR/HSS records for SIM changes.
  • Other platforms include Nokia's Network as Code, Vonage (owned by Ericsson since 2022) and Telefónica's Open Gateway offering; revenue so far is modest compared with operators' core connectivity income.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Treating network APIs as a replacement for all authentication: they are strong signals but should be combined with other fraud checks.
  • Assuming one API works identically everywhere: versions and coverage differ by operator and country, so check availability per market.
  • Ignoring consent and privacy law: location and identity APIs process personal data and need a lawful basis and often user consent.

docs.title: 6.11 5G-Advanced Releases 18, 19 and 20: Timeline and Themes
docs.text:
5G-Advanced is the name for 3GPP Releases 18, 19 and 20 — the second half of 5G's life, bridging to 6G. Release 18 (frozen 2024) introduced AI/ML studies, energy saving, XR and mobility upgrades; Release 19 (frozen December 2025) turned many studies into features; Release 20 (due 2027) finishes 5G-Advanced while 3GPP studies 6G, which becomes normative in Release 21.

5G-Advanced and the road to 6G. Release 20 runs two tracks: finishing 5G-Advanced and studying 6G.

Think of it like…

If 5G is a smartphone model, 5G-Advanced is the 'Pro' refresh: the same family, with smarter software, better battery life and a camera upgrade, before the next generation arrives.

Real-world example

Sofia, a graduate engineer at a fictional vendor, is asked when customers can expect AI-based beam management. She checks the release plan: studied in Rel-18, specified in Rel-19 (frozen December 2025, ASN.1 in 2026), so commercial devices and networks may support it roughly 18-36 months after freeze.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Operators and vendors propose study items and work items at 3GPP plenaries.
  2. Stage 1 defines service requirements, stage 2 the architecture, stage 3 the detailed protocols.
  3. A release is 'frozen' when stage 3 is complete; ASN.1 and OpenAPI code freezes follow about three months later.
  4. Chipset and network vendors implement features; operators test and launch, typically one to three years after freeze.
  5. Later releases add enhancements and corrections; features may be optional, so not every network supports everything.

Who uses it

Standards engineers and delegates, product managers at vendors and operators, technology strategists and students learning 3GPP.

Key takeaway

Remember: 5G-Advanced = Rel-18, 19, 20; 6G normative work starts in Rel-21 (stage 3 freeze planned December 2028, ASN.1 March 2029).

Going deeper

  • 3GPP adopted the name '5G-Advanced' in April 2021 and held a Rel-18 RAN workshop in June 2021 that gathered hundreds of company proposals, later packaged into study and work items.
  • Rel-18 themes included AI/ML for the air interface (study), network energy saving, XR, L1/L2-triggered mobility, eRedCap, NTN enhancements, sidelink evolution, network-controlled repeaters, carrier-phase positioning and UAV support.
  • Rel-19 (frozen at the December 2025 plenaries) delivered AI/ML for beam management and positioning, ambient IoT, regenerative NTN payloads, low-power wake-up signals, sub-band full duplex, further energy savings and channel modelling for 7-24 GHz and ISAC.
  • Rel-20 has two tracks: 5G-Advanced normative work (stage 3 freeze planned March 2027, ASN.1 June 2027) and 6G study items producing technical reports, with stage 1 frozen in June 2025.
  • GSA counted 39 operators investing in 5G-Advanced and seven with launched networks in mid-2026; China Mobile and other Chinese operators were early to market with 5G-A branded launches from 2024.
  • Specification numbers stay the same across releases (e.g. TS 38.331 for RRC); the version number's first digit indicates the release (e.g. 18.x.x for Rel-18).

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming a frozen release means immediate availability: devices and networks typically take one to three years to support new features.
  • Thinking every 5G-Advanced feature will be deployed: many features are optional and some never reach commercial products.
  • Confusing Rel-20's 6G studies with 6G specifications: Rel-20 produces only 6G technical reports; normative 6G specs come in Rel-21.

docs.title: Try it: Decode a 3GPP spec version: the first number is the release
docs.text:
def describe(spec, version):
    major, minor, edit = (int(x) for x in version.split("."))
    return f"TS {spec} v{version}: Release {major}, technical version {minor}, editorial {edit}"

print(describe("38.331", "18.6.0"))   # RRC, Rel-18
print(describe("38.300", "19.1.0"))   # NR overall description, Rel-19

docs.title: 6.12 AI/ML in the Air Interface and RAN (Rel-18 to Rel-20)
docs.text:
5G-Advanced brings machine learning into the radio standards themselves. Phones and base stations can use trained models to predict the best beam, compress channel information, or estimate position more accurately. 3GPP's job is not to standardise the models but the 'plumbing': what data is collected, how models are identified, monitored and switched off if they misbehave.

AI/ML model lifecycle management. Standards focus on lifecycle 'plumbing', not on the model internals.

Think of it like…

It is like teaching a waiter to anticipate orders: the restaurant does not standardise the waiter's brain, but it does set rules for taking notes, checking orders and calling the manager when something goes wrong.

Real-world example

Ravi, a modem engineer at a fictional chipmaker, trains a model that predicts the best of 64 base-station beams by measuring only 8. In a Rel-19 network, the phone reports its predictions, the gNB checks accuracy against occasional full sweeps, and if accuracy drops — say in a new city — the model is deactivated and the phone falls back to classic beam sweeping.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Data collection: devices and gNBs gather measurements (beams, CSI, positioning signals) under defined frameworks.
  2. Training: vendors train models offline, often per scenario or region.
  3. Deployment: models are identified (model or functionality IDs) and activated by the network.
  4. Inference: the device or gNB uses the model, e.g. predicting beams in space or time.
  5. Monitoring and fallback: performance is checked; models are switched or deactivated, falling back to legacy methods.

Who uses it

Wireless ML researchers, modem and RAN algorithm engineers, standards delegates and data scientists at vendors.

Key takeaway

Know the three Rel-18 AI/ML use cases: CSI feedback enhancement, beam management and positioning — and that Rel-19 made beam management and positioning normative.

Going deeper

  • The Rel-18 study, captured in TR 38.843, evaluated AI/ML for CSI feedback compression, beam management (spatial and temporal prediction) and positioning, and defined general lifecycle-management concepts.
  • Rel-19 specified one-sided models for beam management (predicting best beams from a subset of measurements) and for positioning (both AI-assisted measurements and direct AI positioning), plus supporting signalling.
  • Two-sided models, such as an autoencoder that compresses CSI on the phone and decompresses it at the gNB, raise inter-vendor training and interoperability problems and stayed in further study in Rel-19.
  • Generalisation is the core challenge: a model trained in one environment can degrade elsewhere, so monitoring, scenario-specific models and fallback are central to the standard.
  • Separately, RAN3 work (study in Rel-17, TR 37.817; normative in Rel-18) supports AI/ML-based network energy saving, load balancing and mobility optimisation inside NG-RAN, exchanging predictions between nodes.
  • In the management layer, SA5 defines AI/ML management and management data analytics (MDAS), while the 5G core's NWDAF provides analytics; 6G aims to be 'AI-native' across all of these.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking 3GPP standardises neural networks: it standardises data, signalling and lifecycle, while models remain proprietary.
  • Ignoring fallback: every AI/ML feature must degrade gracefully to classic methods when monitoring detects poor performance.
  • Assuming AI/ML always beats conventional algorithms: gains depend on scenario, and overhead for data collection can eat into benefits.

docs.title: 6.13 The 5G-Advanced Feature Toolbox: Mobility, Energy, Coverage, NTN, ISAC
docs.text:
Beyond AI, 5G-Advanced adds many practical upgrades: faster, smoother handovers (LTM), ways for networks and phones to save energy, smart repeaters that extend coverage cheaply, simultaneous send-and-receive within TDD carriers (SBFD), cheaper RedCap devices, better satellite integration, and the first studies on using mobile signals as radar (ISAC).

5G-Advanced feature toolbox. Each feature targets a specific operational pain point.

Think of it like…

If 5G is a car, 5G-Advanced is a mid-life upgrade package: better suspension (mobility), a hybrid engine (energy saving), extra mirrors (repeaters) and parking sensors (sensing).

Real-world example

Fictional operator Andes Móvil plans 2027 upgrades. LTM cuts handover interruptions for passengers on Lima's metro; network-controlled repeaters fill coverage holes on hillside streets at a fraction of a small cell's cost; cell DTX/DRX lowers night-time energy; low-power wake-up signals extend smartwatch battery life.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Identify pain points: mobility interruptions, coverage holes, energy costs, device battery life, uplink delay.
  2. Map them to 5G-Advanced features and the release that introduced them.
  3. Check chipset and network vendor support, since features are optional.
  4. Trial in a cluster, measuring KPIs such as interruption time, coverage, energy and battery life.
  5. Roll out where gains justify cost; plan for later-release enhancements.

Who uses it

RAN product managers, network strategy teams, standards engineers and operator technology planners.

Key takeaway

Pair each feature with its release: LTM, NCR, eRedCap, cell DTX/DRX (Rel-18); LP-WUS, SBFD, regenerative NTN, ISAC channel modelling (Rel-19).

Going deeper

  • L1/L2-triggered mobility (LTM, Rel-18) pre-configures candidate cells and switches using lower-layer signalling, cutting interruption compared with classic layer-3 handover; Rel-19 added conditional LTM and further enhancements.
  • Network-controlled repeaters (NCR, Rel-18) amplify and forward signals but receive beam and timing control from the gNB, unlike 'dumb' RF repeaters that amplify noise and interference in all directions.
  • The Rel-18/19 network energy saving package includes cell DTX/DRX, spatial and power-domain adaptation, and SSB-less secondary cells; Rel-19 added on-demand SSB and further techniques so cells can be quiet more of the time.
  • Low-power wake-up signal (LP-WUS, Rel-19) lets devices keep their main receiver off and listen with an ultra-low-power wake-up receiver, extending battery life for wearables and IoT.
  • Sub-band full duplex (SBFD) lets a gNB receive uplink in part of a TDD carrier while transmitting downlink in the rest; it was studied in Rel-18 and specified in Rel-19, requiring advanced self-interference cancellation at base stations.
  • ISAC (integrated sensing and communication) reached 3GPP through a Rel-19 channel-modelling study for sensing targets such as drones, vehicles and people; Rel-20 continues 5G-Advanced sensing work while 6G studies treat sensing as native.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming repeaters are always cheap wins: unmanaged repeaters can raise interference; NCR's network control exists for this reason.
  • Expecting SBFD in phones: SBFD is a base-station capability; phones still transmit and receive in separate time or frequency resources.
  • Treating ISAC as ready for deployment: in 5G-Advanced it is mainly modelling and studies; real services depend on regulation and privacy.

docs.title: 6.14 5G Scorecard 2026: What Delivered and What Did Not
docs.text:
Seven years after launch, 5G is a big success in coverage, speed and capacity, and has created a real home-broadband business through FWA. But many 2019 promises — new revenue from slicing, mass URLLC, smart everything — arrived slowly or not at all. Understanding this gap explains why operators approach 6G more cautiously.

5G: promise versus 2026 reality

2019 promise 2026 reality Speed Up to 20 Gbit/s Typically hundreds of Mbit/s on mid-band Latency 1 ms URLLC everywhere ~10-30 ms typical; URLLC in niches Massive IoT 1M devices/km² Mostly NB-IoT/LTE-M; RedCap starting Network slicing Big new revenue Few commercial slices (e.g. first responders) Home broadband Side benefit FWA a major success 5G core (SA) Standard by early 2020s ~29% of 5G deployments SA (Q1 2026) Operator revenue New growth era Mostly flat; costs under pressure

Technology largely delivered; new business models lagged.

Think of it like…

5G is like a new motorway network: traffic flows better and new suburbs (FWA) grew along it, but the predicted flying cars and toll-paying robot lorries mostly have not shown up yet.

Real-world example

Hana, an analyst at a fictional investment firm, compares a European operator's 2019 investor deck with 2026 results. Mobile data traffic tripled and 5G coverage passed 90% of the population, but service revenue barely grew. FWA and network APIs add some revenue; slicing and enterprise URLLC contributed little. She concludes that 6G must cut costs, not just add speed.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. List 2019 promises: 10-100x speeds, 1 ms latency, a million devices per km², slicing revenue, smart industries.
  2. Check delivery: subscriptions, coverage, traffic, speeds, SA adoption and new services.
  3. Separate technology capability from commercial uptake.
  4. Identify root causes: slow SA rollout, device ecosystems, business models, spectrum and costs.
  5. Draw lessons for 6G: focus on efficiency, real customer needs and operator economics.

Who uses it

Strategy analysts, operator executives, investors, policymakers and anyone answering 'Was 5G worth it?' in an interview.

Key takeaway

Remember two 2026 data points: over 3 billion 5G subscriptions (Q1 2026, Ericsson) and about 98 operators with 5G SA launched or soft-launched (GSA, August 2026) out of several hundred 5G operators.

Going deeper

  • Ericsson's June 2026 Mobility Report said global 5G subscriptions passed 3 billion in Q1 2026, making 5G the fastest-adopted mobile generation in subscriber terms.
  • GSA's Q1 2026 report counted 95 operators with 5G SA service (29% of 5G deployments, versus 71% NSA); its August 2026 snapshot listed 98 operators with launched or soft-launched SA networks.
  • Many advanced features — slicing, URLLC, RedCap, most 5G-Advanced — need 5G SA, so slow SA adoption directly delayed the services that were meant to bring new revenue.
  • mmWave fell short of early expectations outside specific venues and FWA, while mid-band (3.5 GHz, C-band, 2.5 GHz) became the true 5G workhorse.
  • Operators' capital spending peaked during early 5G rollout and then fell, contributing to the RAN market declines of 2023-2024 and the flat outlook Dell'Oro forecast for 2026.
  • Lessons applied to 6G planning include reusing existing sites and spectrum, prioritising energy efficiency and automation, building on 5G SA cores, and avoiding over-promising use cases before business models exist.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Calling 5G a failure: coverage, capacity, speed and FWA are clear successes; the shortfall is mainly in new revenue streams.
  • Blaming technology alone: device ecosystems, spectrum costs, regulation and enterprise buying cycles also slowed new services.
  • Comparing marketing peak figures with real medians: always compare like with like when judging promises.

docs.title: Chapter 8: 6G: The Next Generation
docs.text: 6G is being designed right now, for launch around 2030. This chapter explains the ITU's IMT-2030 vision and approval process, 3GPP's timeline from Release 20 studies to Release 21 specifications (as agreed by autumn 2026), the early design decisions and migration debate, and candidate spectrum heading into WRC-27. It then explores the key technologies — AI-native radio, sensing, smart surfaces and cell-free MIMO, integrated satellites, new waveforms, digital twins, sustainability and security — the worldwide research ecosystem, and how to tell real progress from hype.

docs.title: 8.1 Why 6G? The IMT-2030 Vision
docs.text:
6G is the mobile generation now being designed for launch around 2030. The ITU's framework, Recommendation ITU-R M.2160 (2023), sets out what it should do: grow 5G's three usage scenarios into six, adding AI, sensing and coverage everywhere, while being sustainable, secure and inclusive. In short, a network that communicates, senses and computes.

The six IMT-2030 usage scenarios. Three scenarios extend 5G's eMBB, URLLC and mMTC; three are new for 6G.

Think of it like…

If 5G built faster motorways, 6G aims to make the motorways smart infrastructure that also watches traffic, predicts jams and reaches remote villages — while using less energy per car.

Real-world example

Amara, a planner at the fictional Port of Kessa, reads the IMT-2030 framework to see what 2030s networks could offer: remote crane control with immersive video (Immersive Communication + HRLLC), drone tracking from base stations (ISAC) and coverage for ships offshore (Ubiquitous Connectivity).

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. ITU-R Working Party 5D studied technology trends (Report ITU-R M.2516, 2022) and agreed the IMT-2030 framework in 2023.
  2. Recommendation M.2160, approved in November 2023, defines six usage scenarios, four overarching aspects and fifteen capabilities with indicative target ranges.
  3. ITU then writes binding minimum requirements and evaluation rules, while 3GPP studies the technology (Release 20).
  4. Technology proposals are submitted to ITU from February 2027, evaluated, and approved as IMT-2030 around 2030.
  5. Operators launch commercial 6G from about 2030, gradually, alongside 5G-Advanced.

Who uses it

Technology strategists, standards delegates, researchers, regulators and vendor product planners.

Key takeaway

Name the six scenarios: Immersive Communication, HRLLC and Massive Communication (evolved from 5G) plus Ubiquitous Connectivity, AI and Communication, and Integrated Sensing and Communication (new).

Going deeper

  • M.2160's four overarching aspects apply to every scenario: sustainability, connecting the unconnected, ubiquitous intelligence, and security, privacy and resilience.
  • Indicative capability ranges include peak data rates of 50, 100 or 200 Gbit/s, user-experienced rates of 300-500 Mbit/s, latency of 0.1-1 ms and connection density of 10^6 to 10^8 devices per km².
  • Reliability targets range from 1-10^-5 to 1-10^-7, and mobility from 500 to 1,000 km/h — covering high-speed trains and, potentially, aircraft.
  • New capabilities with no 5G equivalent include positioning (indicative 1-10 cm accuracy), sensing-related capabilities, AI-related capabilities, coverage, interoperability and sustainability.
  • The framework gives ranges, not pass/fail values; binding minimum requirements come in the separate technical performance requirements report, drafted in February 2026 with 20 requirements.
  • Operator groups such as NGMN stress that 6G must lower cost and energy and simplify migration, rather than chase headline peak rates — a lesson from slow 5G returns.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Quoting '1 Tbit/s' as the 6G target — that came from early research papers; M.2160 lists up to 200 Gbit/s as an indicative peak.
  • Thinking 6G replaces 5G overnight — 5G-Advanced keeps evolving and 6G will roll out gradually from about 2030.
  • Treating the six scenarios as six separate networks — one 6G system is expected to serve all of them.

docs.title: 8.2 The ITU IMT-2030 Process: Requirements, Submissions and Approval
docs.text:
The ITU does not design 6G itself. It sets requirements, invites technology proposals, has independent groups evaluate them, and then approves those that pass as IMT-2030. As of October 2026, the minimum-requirements and evaluation-guideline reports are drafted and waiting for approval in December 2026, and the window for submitting proposals opens in February 2027.

From vision to approved IMT-2030 technology. In October 2026 the process sits between requirements (approval due December 2026) and submissions (opening February 2027).

Think of it like…

It is like an architecture competition: the city publishes the brief and judging rules, teams submit designs within a window, independent judges score them, and the winners receive the official seal.

Real-world example

Joon, a standards engineer at the fictional Hanul Electronics, maps his company's path: its ideas go into 3GPP Release 21, 3GPP's partners submit the result to ITU-R WP 5D before the February 2029 deadline, and independent evaluation groups check it against 20 minimum requirements in seven test environments.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Vision and framework: Recommendation M.2160 (2023) defines scenarios and capabilities.
  2. Requirements and evaluation: the technical performance requirements report (drafted February 2026) and evaluation guidelines (drafted June 2026) go to Study Group 5 for approval in December 2026; a submission-template report is still being finalised.
  3. Call for proposals: Circular Letter 5/LCCE/115, published in late 2024, invites candidate radio interface technologies.
  4. Submissions: accepted from WP 5D meeting #54 (February 2027) until shortly before meeting #59 (February 2029).
  5. Evaluation and consensus run through 2029, leading to IMT-2030 Recommendation(s) with detailed specifications around 2030.

Who uses it

Standards and regulatory engineers, members of evaluation groups at universities and institutes, and government delegates.

Key takeaway

ITU sets requirements and approves; 3GPP writes the technology. 3GPP's proposal reaches ITU through its organisational partners such as ATIS and ETSI.

Going deeper

  • The draft technical performance requirements report defines 20 minimum requirements: 14 evolved from IMT-2020 (such as peak rate, spectral efficiency, latency, reliability, mobility and energy efficiency) and 6 new ones (including positioning, sensing, AI and resilience).
  • Evaluation guidelines plan seven test environments, including indoor hotspot, dense urban, rural, urban macro, an indoor factory for HRLLC, and two ISAC environments (indoor factory and urban macro).
  • Report ITU-R M.2541 (2024) examined the technical feasibility of IMT in bands above 100 GHz, an important input for sub-THz research.
  • The submission deadline is 12 days before the start of WP 5D meeting #59 in February 2029, which 3GPP's Release 21 schedule (ASN.1 freeze March 2029) was planned to meet with an early-2029 submission.
  • For 5G, Recommendation ITU-R M.2150 with the detailed IMT-2020 specifications was first approved in February 2021, more than a year after commercial launches — 6G is expected to follow a similar pattern.
  • WP 5D's 53rd meeting (late September to early October 2026) continued work on the remaining submission and evaluation-process documents before the window opens.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking ITU invents 6G technology — ITU sets requirements and approves; 3GPP and others design the radio interfaces.
  • Confusing the framework (M.2160) with minimum requirements — the framework gives ranges; the requirements report gives pass/fail values.
  • Assuming only 3GPP can submit — any ITU member or recognised organisation may propose a radio interface technology.

docs.title: 8.3 3GPP's Road to 6G: Release 20 Studies to Release 21 Specifications
docs.text:
3GPP is writing 6G in two phases. Release 20 (2025-2027) is the study phase, with study items on requirements, radio, architecture, security and more. Release 21 is the first normative 6G release: work items start in March 2027, specifications freeze in stages through December 2028, and the final ASN.1/OpenAPI code freezes in March 2029, ahead of commercial launches expected around 2030.

3GPP 6G milestones (as agreed by September 2026). Dates after 2026 are plans agreed at the June 2026 plenaries; 3GPP has moved dates before.

Think of it like…

Like building a new airport: first feasibility studies and design workshops (Release 20), then detailed blueprints frozen phase by phase (Release 21), then construction and opening day (2030).

Real-world example

The fictional chipmaker Lumo Semi plans its first 6G modem: it follows radio decisions through 2027-2028, prototypes against the June 2028 architecture freeze, finalises silicon after the December 2028 protocol freeze and targets phones launching in 2030.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. March 2025: a dedicated 3GPP 6G workshop in Incheon, Korea gathers company views on scope and priorities.
  2. June 2025: the RAN plenary approves the 6G radio study; SA groups run studies on use cases, architecture, security and more in Release 20.
  3. March 2026: SA approves TR 22.870 (6G use cases and service requirements); June 2026: RAN approves TR 38.914 (6G scenarios and requirements) and the full Release 21 timeline.
  4. March 2027: Release 21 work items approved and Stage 1 frozen; RAN1 normative work runs roughly Q2 2027 to Q3 2028.
  5. March 2028: 80% Stage 2 checkpoint; June 2028: Stage 2 freeze; December 2028: Stage 3 freeze; March 2029: ASN.1/OpenAPI freeze.

Who uses it

Standards engineers, product planners, chip and device makers, and operators' technology-strategy teams.

Key takeaway

Release 20 = 6G studies plus the last purely 5G-Advanced work; Release 21 = the first 6G specifications (plus more 5G-Advanced).

Going deeper

  • Release 20 6G studies include FS_6G_REQ (SA1, TR 22.870), FS_6G_RAN_Scen_Req (TR 38.914), FS_6G_Radio (RAN), FS_6G_ARC (SA2), FS_6G_SEC (SA3), and studies on media, charging, management, lawful interception, mission-critical services and application enablement.
  • At the June 2026 plenaries (TSGs#112, Singapore) 3GPP fixed Release 21: Stage 1 freeze March 2027, 80% Stage 2 checkpoint March 2028, Stage 2 freeze June 2028, Stage 3 freeze December 2028, ASN.1/OpenAPI freeze March 2029.
  • Trade-press reports of the timeline put RAN1 normative work at roughly Q2 2027 to Q3 2028 and RAN2-4 at Q3 2027 to Q4 2028, with an extra quarter to review ASN.1 and APIs.
  • Working-group capacity is shared between 5G-Advanced and 6G, so 3GPP avoids overlapping scope; the March 2026 Release 20 work plan listed about 200 work and study items in total.
  • The O-RAN Alliance began 6G study work in February 2026, splitting work so that the air interface stays in 3GPP and open fronthaul is specified by O-RAN, possibly three to six months behind 3GPP.
  • For comparison, 5G had Release 14 studies (2016-2017), Release 15 specifications (2018-2019) and first launches in 2019; 6G plans a similar gap between specs and service.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Calling Release 20 'the 6G release' — it contains 6G studies only; the first 6G specifications are in Release 21.
  • Expecting 6G phones in 2028 — specifications complete only in early 2029, so commercial devices are expected around 2030.
  • Treating freeze dates as fixed forever — 3GPP has shifted dates before; always check the latest plenary decisions.

docs.title: 8.4 The 6G Radio and System Take Shape: Early Decisions and Migration
docs.text:
By late 2026 3GPP had already settled several basics for 6G. It reuses proven 5G building blocks — CP-OFDM, 5G channel codes and a similar frame structure — and changes what matters: wider carriers up to 400 MHz, better uplink, massive IoT built in from day one and deeper energy savings. The big open debate is migration: how 6G will share spectrum and work alongside 5G.

5G NR vs 6G as agreed or studied in 2026

5G NR (Rel-15) 6G (2026 study status) Downlink waveform CP-OFDM CP-OFDM Uplink waveform CP-OFDM; DFT-s-OFDM 1 layer CP-OFDM; DFT-s-OFDM with MIMO Max carrier, mid-band 100 MHz up to 400 MHz (3-400 MHz range) Channel codes LDPC + polar largely reused, enhanced Massive IoT via LTE-M / NB-IoT built in from the start Launch mode NSA first, SA later standalone baseline Sharing older generation DSS with LTE overhead MRSS designed in

Most changes target cost, coverage, energy and smoother migration rather than a new radio from scratch.

Think of it like…

Like designing a new car model that keeps the proven engine and gearbox but adds a new battery, sensors and software — and it must share the roads with older cars from day one.

Real-world example

The fictional operator Brightwave carries 5G on 100 MHz at 3.5 GHz. With multi-RAT spectrum sharing it can give part of that carrier to 6G dynamically as 6G phones appear, instead of clearing the band first — while its new 7 GHz spectrum carries 6G capacity from launch.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Waveforms: CP-OFDM for the downlink; CP-OFDM and DFT-s-OFDM for the uplink, with DFT-s-OFDM now usable with uplink MIMO.
  2. Carrier bandwidths from 3 MHz to 400 MHz depending on the band (5G's mid-band maximum is 100 MHz).
  3. Channel coding largely reused from 5G (LDPC for data, polar for control) with enhancements under study; uniform QAM as the modulation basis.
  4. Frame structure similar to 5G to allow sharing; longer reference-signal and system-information periods studied for energy savings.
  5. Architecture: standalone 6G with a new core; base station as one unit or split into CU and DU; lower-layer split detailed by O-RAN.
  6. Migration: multi-RAT spectrum sharing (MRSS) with 5G, plus options such as 6G-anchored dual connectivity with 5G still under discussion.

Who uses it

RAN and core architects, operator technology-strategy teams, chipset designers and standards delegates.

Key takeaway

6G reuses more of 5G than 5G reused of 4G — the goal is cheaper evolution, not a total redesign.

Going deeper

  • Allowing DFT-s-OFDM with uplink MIMO is a change from 5G, aimed at better cell-edge coverage where a phone's power amplifier is the bottleneck.
  • The 3-400 MHz bandwidth range lets 6G fit narrow refarmed low bands and the wide channels expected around 7-15 GHz; one 400 MHz carrier needs less carrier-aggregation complexity than four 100 MHz carriers.
  • The RAN-core interface is planned as point-to-point, with protocols still to be decided; non-connectivity services such as sensing will be handled alongside their functionality.
  • Operators in NGMN (2026 papers) urged simplicity: one standalone architecture, MRSS as the baseline migration and no repeat of 5G's many NSA/SA options.
  • At the September 2026 plenaries, reports say discussion focused on two options — 6G-anchored dual connectivity with 5G NR and a dual-stack approach without RAN-level aggregation — with RAN1 presenting preliminary MRSS overhead results.
  • MRSS aims to let 5G and 6G share a carrier without the always-on LTE reference signals that made 4G/5G DSS costly; its overhead study ran to September 2026.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming 6G needs new spectrum before launch — MRSS lets 6G start in existing 5G bands and grow as devices arrive.
  • Thinking 6G repeats 5G's NSA path — the baseline is standalone with a 6G core; any 5G interworking is deliberately kept simple.
  • Treating study conclusions as final specifications — details can still change during Release 21 normative work.

docs.title: 8.5 Spectrum for 6G: Upper Mid-Band, Sub-THz and WRC-27
docs.text:
6G will start in today's mobile bands, shared with 5G, but it needs new wide channels for capacity. The industry's favourite is the upper mid-band, roughly 7-15 GHz (often called FR3), which balances coverage and bandwidth. Frequencies above 100 GHz (sub-THz) offer enormous bandwidth for short links. WRC-27 in Shanghai (October-November 2027) will decide on key candidate bands.

Bandwidth on offer in candidate 6G ranges. Each step up in frequency multiplies the available bandwidth — and the propagation challenge.

Think of it like…

Low bands are long country roads, mid-band is the city ring road, the upper mid-band is a new multi-lane motorway being planned, and sub-THz is a super-fast but very short airport walkway.

Real-world example

The regulator of the fictional country Valdoria plans for 6G: it keeps 3.5 GHz for 5G/6G sharing, studies 7.125-8.4 GHz with its defence ministry, which runs satellite links there, and waits for WRC-27 before auctioning 400 MHz blocks.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Reuse existing 5G and 4G bands through MRSS and refarming for coverage and early capacity.
  2. Add new mid-band capacity: upper 6 GHz (6.425-7.125 GHz, identified for IMT in Region 1 at WRC-23) and 7.125-8.4 GHz under WRC-27 agenda item 1.7.
  3. Study further candidates under item 1.7: 4.4-4.8 GHz and 14.8-15.35 GHz.
  4. Keep mmWave (FR2) bands for hotspots and fixed wireless access.
  5. Research sub-THz (roughly 100-300 GHz) for later short-range, very-high-rate links — not a launch band.

Who uses it

Spectrum strategists, RF engineers, regulators, and antenna and chip designers.

Key takeaway

Memorise WRC-27 agenda item 1.7 bands: 4.4-4.8 GHz, 7.125-8.4 GHz and 14.8-15.35 GHz.

Going deeper

  • The upper mid-band combines reasonable propagation with several hundred MHz per operator; with 'giga-MIMO' arrays, vendors aim to reuse today's 3.5 GHz site grid at similar coverage.
  • 7.125-8.4 GHz is heavily used by government and military systems (fixed links, satellites); the US 2023 National Spectrum Strategy listed 7.125-8.4 GHz for study, and the 2025 US budget law excluded 7.4-8.4 GHz from mandated auctions.
  • In Europe the upper 6 GHz band (6.425-7.125 GHz) is contested between Wi-Fi and mobile, and EU-level discussions in 2025-2026 considered how it should be used or split.
  • Sub-THz options such as the D-band (110-170 GHz) and 252-321 GHz (used by IEEE 802.15.3d) offer tens of GHz of bandwidth but face high path loss, absorption and inefficient power amplifiers; ITU-R M.2541 studied feasibility above 100 GHz.
  • Free-space path loss grows by 20 dB per decade of frequency: moving from 3.5 GHz to 140 GHz costs about 32 dB, partly recovered because more antenna elements fit in the same panel size.
  • WRC-27 runs from 18 October to 12 November 2027 in Shanghai; national 6G auctions in the new bands are therefore unlikely before 2028-2029, which fits launch plans around 2030.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking 6G is mainly a terahertz technology — launches focus on existing bands and 7-15 GHz; sub-THz is a later, niche option.
  • Assuming WRC-27 candidate bands are guaranteed for mobile — studies must show coexistence with incumbents, and outcomes may differ by region.
  • Ignoring uplink limits — higher bands shrink uplink coverage, so 6G deployments pair them with lower bands.

docs.title: Try it: Free-space path loss at 200 m for 5G and 6G candidate frequencies
docs.text:
import math
d_km = 0.2
for f_ghz in (0.7, 3.5, 7.5, 15, 28, 140):
    fspl = 20*math.log10(d_km) + 20*math.log10(f_ghz) + 92.45
    print(f"{f_ghz:>6} GHz: {fspl:5.1f} dB")
# +20 dB per 10x frequency; bigger antenna arrays win part of it back

docs.title: 8.6 AI-Native Air Interface and Network
docs.text:
In 5G, artificial intelligence is mostly bolted on. 6G aims to be 'AI-native': designed so machine-learning models can run inside the radio and the core, with standard ways to collect data, train, deploy, monitor and switch models. The network may also offer AI services and carry heavy AI traffic itself.

AI model life-cycle management. The fallback step is what makes AI safe enough for a radio standard.

Think of it like…

Like a smart building designed with sensors, wiring and automation from the blueprint stage, instead of adding gadgets to an old house.

Real-world example

The fictional chipmaker Lumo Semi trains a neural network that compresses channel-state feedback more compactly than 5G's codebooks in simulations. In 6G, the phone and network would agree which model to use, monitor its accuracy and fall back to a classic codebook if performance drops.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Data collection: phones and network gather measurements using standardised reporting.
  2. Training: usually offline at vendors or operators; some models are two-sided (encoder in the phone, decoder in the base station).
  3. Deployment: the model or AI functionality is identified and activated through signalling.
  4. Monitoring: performance is checked continuously; models are switched, updated or deactivated (life-cycle management).
  5. Network AI: core and management functions use analytics and AI agents to automate operations and expose AI services.

Who uses it

Telecom machine-learning engineers, RAN algorithm designers, chipset teams and AI-RAN platform engineers.

Key takeaway

Know the path: Release 18 study (TR 38.843) → Release 19 normative AI for beam management and positioning → 6G designs AI life-cycle management in from the start.

Going deeper

  • 3GPP's Release 18 study TR 38.843 examined three pilot use cases — CSI feedback enhancement, beam management and positioning; Release 19 made AI-based beam management and positioning normative while CSI compression continued as a study.
  • Two-sided models (an encoder in the phone and a decoder in the base station) raise hard interoperability questions: who trains them, how they are tested across vendors, and how models are shared without exposing IP.
  • AI-RAN runs RAN software and AI workloads on shared GPU-accelerated servers; the AI-RAN Alliance launched in February 2024 with founding members including NVIDIA, SoftBank, Ericsson, Nokia, Samsung, Microsoft, Arm and T-Mobile.
  • NVIDIA announced a $1 billion investment in Nokia in October 2025 to co-develop AI-RAN products for 5G-Advanced and 6G, with T-Mobile US planning field trials from 2026.
  • Neural receivers that replace classic channel estimation and detection blocks have shown gains in research, but power consumption, cost and verification on phones remain open issues.
  • On the network side, 6G architecture studies consider AI agents and AI services exposed by the network, building on the NWDAF analytics function introduced in 5G.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking 'AI-native' means everything becomes a neural network — classic algorithms remain the baseline and fallback.
  • Ignoring testability — certifying AI behaviour across millions of devices is much harder than testing fixed algorithms.
  • Assuming training data is free — collecting it costs signalling, battery, storage and privacy compliance.

docs.title: Try it: Toy 'CSI compression': keep only the strongest principal components of a channel matrix
docs.text:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
H = rng.normal(size=(64, 8)) @ rng.normal(size=(8, 32))   # low-rank 'channel'
U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(H, full_matrices=False)
k = 8                                                      # values fed back
H_hat = U[:, :k] @ np.diag(s[:k]) @ Vt[:k]
print('relative error:', np.linalg.norm(H - H_hat) / np.linalg.norm(H))

docs.title: 8.7 Integrated Sensing and Communication (ISAC)
docs.text:
ISAC lets the mobile network work like radar. Base stations, and sometimes phones, analyse reflections of their own radio signals to detect, locate and track objects such as drones, cars or people — while still carrying data. 5G-Advanced is studying first steps; 6G aims to design sensing in from the start as one of its six usage scenarios.

A bistatic sensing request. The target carries no device — the network senses it purely from reflected radio waves.

Think of it like…

Like a bat that uses the same voice both to call its friends and to echolocate insects in the dark.

Real-world example

The fictional SkyPort airport uses a 6G network to spot unauthorised drones near runways. One base station transmits, a second measures the echoes (bistatic sensing), and the network's sensing function reports each drone's position and speed every 100 ms to airport security.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. An authorised application requests sensing, for example 'monitor this area for drones'.
  2. The network's sensing function selects base stations or devices and configures sensing signals, or reuses data signals.
  3. A transmitter sends; a receiver — the same node (monostatic) or another node (bistatic) — captures the echoes.
  4. Processing estimates range from delay, speed from Doppler shift and direction from beams, then tracks objects.
  5. Results are exposed through APIs to authorised users, under privacy and security rules.

Who uses it

Radar and RF engineers, automotive and drone-safety teams, smart-city planners and standards delegates.

Key takeaway

Range resolution ≈ c / (2 × bandwidth): 400 MHz gives about 37.5 cm, so 6G's wider carriers sharpen sensing.

Going deeper

  • 3GPP Release 19 SA1 work (TR 22.837) collected ISAC use cases and requirements — from drone detection and traffic monitoring to intrusion detection and health monitoring.
  • Release 19 RAN work extended 3GPP's channel models (TR 38.901) to include sensing targets such as drones, people and vehicles, so sensing performance can be simulated consistently.
  • ETSI's Industry Specification Group on ISAC, launched in late 2023, publishes reports on use cases, channel modelling and KPIs ahead of formal standards.
  • Monostatic sensing needs strong isolation between transmitter and receiver at the same site (like full duplex); bistatic and multistatic set-ups avoid self-interference but need tight time synchronisation.
  • The IMT-2030 evaluation plans two ISAC test environments, and the requirements include sensing metrics such as accuracy, resolution and detection probability.
  • Privacy is a major issue: sensing can reveal people's presence and movement without any device, so consent, anonymisation and lawful access must be defined before services launch.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming ISAC needs the target to carry a phone — device-free sensing tracks objects that carry nothing.
  • Expecting radar-grade accuracy everywhere — results depend on bandwidth, geometry, clutter and synchronisation.
  • Forgetting that sensing costs capacity — sensing signals use time, frequency and energy that could otherwise carry data.

docs.title: Try it: Range resolution and maximum unambiguous speed for sensing signals
docs.text:
c = 3e8
for bw_mhz in (100, 400, 2000):
    print(f"{bw_mhz} MHz -> range resolution {c/(2*bw_mhz*1e6):.3f} m")
f, slot = 7e9, 125e-6           # 7 GHz carrier, one sensing pulse per 125 µs
v_max = (c/f) / (4*slot)         # max unambiguous radial speed
print(f"max speed ≈ {v_max:.0f} m/s")

docs.title: 8.8 Reconfigurable Surfaces, Cell-Free and Extreme MIMO
docs.text:
6G research is reshaping how antennas serve users. Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS) are smart panels that steer reflected radio waves around obstacles. Cell-free massive MIMO replaces cells with many cooperating access points that jointly serve each user. Extreme or 'giga' MIMO packs hundreds of antenna elements into arrays for the 7-15 GHz range.

Cell-free MIMO with a RIS assist. Users are served jointly by several access points; the RIS adds a controllable reflected path around a blockage.

Think of it like…

A RIS is like a set of adjustable mirrors bouncing sunlight into a shaded courtyard; cell-free MIMO is like a choir where every singer adjusts so each listener hears the best blend, instead of one soloist per room.

Real-world example

In the fictional Harborview metro, a RIS panel on a tunnel wall redirects a 7 GHz beam around a bend, while in the main concourse 32 small access points act as one cell-free system — so passengers see similar speeds wherever they stand, with no cell edges.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. RIS: a controller sets each element's phase so reflections add up towards the intended user.
  2. Cell-free: many access points connect over fronthaul to a central processing unit; each user is served by a cluster of nearby access points.
  3. Precoding is computed jointly so access points cancel interference between users.
  4. Giga-MIMO: large arrays form narrow, high-gain beams that restore coverage at higher frequencies.
  5. Near-field effects: with very large arrays at short range, beams can focus on a point rather than just a direction.

Who uses it

Antenna and RF front-end engineers, RAN researchers, indoor-coverage planners and chip designers.

Key takeaway

A RIS is (mostly) passive and has no power amplifier, unlike a repeater; 3GPP Release 18 standardised network-controlled repeaters, not RIS.

Going deeper

  • A RIS contains hundreds to thousands of sub-wavelength elements whose reflection phase is switched with PIN diodes, varactors or liquid crystal; because it cannot amplify, the path losses of both hops multiply.
  • ETSI ISG RIS, started in 2021, has published reports on use cases, channel models and architecture; 3GPP has not standardised RIS, but Release 18 network-controlled repeaters (NCR) are a stepping stone.
  • NTT DOCOMO and AGC demonstrated a transparent metasurface in 2020 that could pass, block or reflect 28 GHz signals, hinting at windows that manage indoor coverage.
  • Cell-free massive MIMO, formalised in research around 2017, removes cell-edge effects but needs heavy fronthaul and tight synchronisation; scalable versions limit each user to a cluster of nearby access points.
  • Vendors' giga-MIMO concepts for 7-15 GHz place many hundreds of elements in a panel similar in size to today's 3.5 GHz radios, so extra beamforming gain offsets higher path loss.
  • The near-field boundary 2D²/λ grows with array size: a 1 m array at 15 GHz has a near field reaching about 100 m, enabling beam focusing on a spot rather than only a direction.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking RIS gives free coverage — it needs control signalling and careful placement, and it cannot amplify signals.
  • Calling any distributed antenna system 'cell-free' — cell-free requires joint, coherent processing of each user across access points.
  • Ignoring cost and power — thousands of fully digital RF chains are impractical, so hybrid beamforming remains essential.

docs.title: Try it: How far the 'near field' of a large array reaches (Fraunhofer distance 2D²/λ)
docs.text:
c = 3e8
for f_ghz, D in ((3.5, 0.5), (7.5, 0.5), (15, 1.0), (140, 0.2)):
    lam = c / (f_ghz * 1e9)
    print(f"{f_ghz} GHz, {D} m array: near field up to {2*D**2/lam:.0f} m")

docs.title: 8.9 Integrated Terrestrial and Non-Terrestrial 6G
docs.text:
6G aims to make satellites, high-altitude platforms and ground networks work as one system, so a phone can move between a tower and a satellite seamlessly and remote places get coverage. 5G added non-terrestrial support from Release 17 as an extension; 6G plans it in the base design, with the same air interface, core and management.

The 6G multi-layer network. Each layer trades coverage area against capacity and delay; 6G aims to manage them as one network.

Think of it like…

Like an airline alliance with one ticket covering trains, short flights and long-haul routes — the traveller just moves, and the system picks each leg.

Real-world example

A crew member on the fictional trawler Atlantica uses a 6G phone connected to a low-Earth-orbit satellite 300 km offshore. Near port, the same phone and SIM hand over to the coastal 6G tower without the crew noticing anything.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Terrestrial cells serve populated areas; high-altitude platforms fill regional gaps; LEO satellites cover oceans, deserts and disaster zones.
  2. Satellites with regenerative payloads run base-station functions in orbit and relay through optical inter-satellite links.
  3. The unified air interface and core handle mobility, timing and Doppler compensation across all layers.
  4. Spectrum combines satellite bands with terrestrial bands for direct-to-device links, subject to regulation.
  5. The network chooses which layer serves each user for coverage, capacity and resilience.

Who uses it

Satellite and NTN engineers, operators' rural-coverage teams, emergency services, and maritime and aviation industries.

Key takeaway

Ubiquitous Connectivity is one of the six IMT-2030 usage scenarios — so non-terrestrial integration is central to 6G, not an add-on.

Going deeper

  • 3GPP Release 17 introduced NR-NTN and IoT-NTN with transparent (bent-pipe) payloads; Releases 18 and 19 added coverage enhancements, bands above 10 GHz and regenerative payload support; 6G aims to support NTN natively.
  • LEO links add only a few milliseconds of one-way delay but large, fast-changing Doppler shifts (tens of kHz at 2 GHz), which devices pre-compensate using GNSS position and satellite orbit data.
  • WRC-23 approved high-altitude IMT base stations (HIBS) at about 20 km in some existing IMT bands below 2.7 GHz, offering regional coverage from the stratosphere.
  • WRC-27 agenda item 1.13 studies satellite direct-to-device links in IMT bands between 694 MHz and 2.7 GHz, which could replace national waivers with global rules.
  • Europe's IRIS² constellation (planned around 2030) and China's large LEO constellations such as Guowang and Qianfan are expected to interact with 6G non-terrestrial plans.
  • Integration challenges include handover between layers, spectrum sharing between satellite and terrestrial users, and scheduling links whose delays differ by orders of magnitude.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Expecting satellite links to match towers — phone-to-satellite links have tight power budgets; early direct-to-device offers messaging and modest data.
  • Thinking non-terrestrial networks replace terrestrial ones — satellites fill gaps; dense areas still need cells.
  • Ignoring regulation — direct-to-device use of terrestrial spectrum needs national approval until global rules exist.

docs.title: 8.10 〰️ New Waveforms, Terahertz Hardware and Semantic Communication
docs.text:
Researchers are exploring what might follow OFDM in extreme conditions: waveforms such as OTFS and AFDM cope with very fast movement, sub-terahertz radios need new low-power hardware, and semantic communication sends the meaning of data rather than every bit. Because 3GPP chose CP-OFDM for 6G's start, these are mostly longer-term research topics.

Waveform options for 6G and beyond

CP-OFDM OTFS / AFDM Single-carrier (sub-THz) Strength simple, MIMO-friendly robust to high Doppler low PAPR, efficient PAs Weakness Doppler, high PAPR complex receivers harder multi-user scheduling Status agreed for 6G research research Best fit most bands trains, aircraft, LEO 100-300 GHz links

CP-OFDM won the 6G baseline; the others target special conditions such as high speed or sub-THz.

Think of it like…

Semantic communication is like texting 'same as last week' instead of resending the whole shopping list — the receiver's knowledge fills in the rest.

Real-world example

The fictional university lab NovaWave simulates a train at 500 km/h. OFDM subcarriers smear because of Doppler, while AFDM keeps errors lower in its tests — but the lab notes the receiver is more complex and that 6G will start with CP-OFDM anyway.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Identify a limit of CP-OFDM — high Doppler, high peak-to-average power, or phase noise at sub-THz.
  2. Propose an alternative — OTFS (delay-Doppler domain), AFDM (chirps), or single-carrier waveforms for sub-THz.
  3. Evaluate in simulators and prototypes, weighing gains against complexity and compatibility.
  4. For semantic communication, train joint source-channel codecs end to end.
  5. Standards adopt only techniques that clearly beat OFDM at acceptable cost.

Who uses it

Wireless researchers, PhD students, DSP engineers and RF hardware designers.

Key takeaway

For exams: OTFS places symbols in the delay-Doppler domain; PAPR matters because power amplifiers waste energy on peaky signals.

Going deeper

  • OTFS, proposed in 2017, spreads each symbol across the whole time-frequency grid so every symbol sees the full channel; at high Doppler it can beat OFDM, at the cost of complex equalisers.
  • AFDM uses chirp-based subcarriers and is studied as a more OFDM-compatible alternative for high-mobility links such as trains and satellites.
  • Sub-THz transceivers struggle with low power-amplifier efficiency, strong phase noise and power-hungry converters; designs explore 1-4-bit ADCs and single-carrier waveforms to save power.
  • IEEE 802.15.3d (2017) is the first wireless standard for 252-321 GHz, targeting 100 Gbit/s point-to-point links for data centres, fronthaul and kiosks.
  • Semantic and goal-oriented communication use deep joint source-channel coding so images degrade gracefully rather than failing at a cliff; standardisation is far off because meaning depends on shared models.
  • NTT DOCOMO, NTT, NEC and Fujitsu jointly demonstrated about 100 Gbit/s wireless transmission in the 100 GHz and 300 GHz bands in 2024.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Believing OFDM is dead in 6G — 3GPP agreed CP-OFDM for the downlink and as an uplink option.
  • Thinking semantic communication avoids bits — data still travels as bits; the gain comes from choosing which bits matter.
  • Underestimating hardware — sub-THz chips, packaging and power consumption limit progress more than theory does.

docs.title: Try it: Compare the peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR) of OFDM and a single-carrier signal
docs.text:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
qpsk = (rng.choice([-1, 1], 1024) + 1j*rng.choice([-1, 1], 1024)) / np.sqrt(2)
ofdm = np.fft.ifft(qpsk) * np.sqrt(1024)
papr = lambda x: 10*np.log10(np.max(abs(x)**2) / np.mean(abs(x)**2))
print(f"single-carrier QPSK: {papr(qpsk):.1f} dB, OFDM: {papr(ofdm):.1f} dB")

Goal-oriented communicationResearch · Concept · Research · 6G Designing transmission to achieve a task, such as controlling a robot, rather than maximising raw throughput. A robot arm receives only the control updates that change its next movement. Deep JSCCResearch · Technology · Research · 6G Deep joint source-channel coding: neural networks map data directly to radio symbols, avoiding the 'cliff effect'. As signal quality drops, a deep-JSCC video call blurs gradually instead of freezing. A hospital ward uses Li-Fi lamps to avoid radio interference with equipment. A full-duplex gNB serves downlink and uplink at once, halving delay for industrial control.
